titleEn: Choking in a Restaurant - FBAO That Progresses to Cardiac Arrest

patient.name: Raymond Cole
patient.affectEn: Stage 1 (partial obstruction): standing beside the table, red-faced and frightened, coughing forcefully with high-pitched noises, still moving some air. Stage 2 (complete obstruction): silent and wide-eyed with both hands gripping his throat, lips turning blue. Stage 3 (collapse): limp and unresponsive, no chest movement, dusky. After ROSC: drowsy, hoarse and confused, pale, cool and sweaty, with a sore breastbone and upper belly.
patient.speechEn: Stage 1: he can only whisper a single word (steak). Stage 2: no voice at all. Stage 3: none. After ROSC: a few hoarse words at a time, confused about the last few minutes, repeating what happened? If asked his name he gives it. The history comes mainly from his wife, who is panicking at first and then frightened but answers exactly what she is asked.

scene.settingEn: A busy steakhouse in Langley at 1912 hrs. Music is playing and diners stand in a loose circle around a corner table. The floor is clear tile, the table has been cleared and the chairs pushed back; no spills and no other hazards. One patient. The hospital is 11 minutes away.
hazardsEn: none identified - clear tile floor, table cleared, chairs pushed back, no spills

bystanders.knowsEn: Beside him, panicking. They were out for their anniversary dinner. He was talking and laughing, swallowed a large piece of steak without chewing, and started coughing at about 1910; he could not clear it. Nobody touched him before you arrived and he did not lose consciousness until the collapse. Only if asked: high blood pressure and high cholesterol, no heart or lung disease, no swallowing problems and no previous choking; ramipril and atorvastatin, no blood thinners; allergic to penicillin (rash); bread and salad, then the steak, and two glasses of red wine, nothing since the steak. She will do simple tasks if told and needs someone to stay with her.
Made the 911 call: the man swallowed a piece of steak, nobody has touched him, and the restaurant has no AED. Will hold doors, bring the cot and clear the space if asked.
A loose circle of diners. They step back and give you room when asked and do not touch the patient.

Exist only if the candidate asked dispatch for them: dispatch replies Copy and says they are on the way; no arrival time is given. They are not on scene during the first two minutes of CPR. Once they are there they take over compressions on direction.

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation. Carries the AED, suction, BVM and oxygen.
equipmentEn: AED (carried by your partner; the restaurant has none)
adult BVM with oxygen tubing and reservoir
PCP only: IV start kit and supraglottic airway

dispatchEn: 1912 hrs. Code 3 to a steakhouse in Langley. A 58-year-old male is choking on food. The server who called says he is coughing, cannot speak properly and is getting worse. Hospital is 11 minutes away.
dispatchUpdateEn: Dispatch update en route: the server says the man swallowed a piece of steak, nobody has touched him, and the restaurant has no AED.
arrivalEn: Busy steakhouse dining room with music playing; diners stand in a loose circle around a corner table. A woman beside the patient is panicking and tells you he swallowed a large piece of steak without chewing. The floor is clear tile, the table is cleared and the chairs are pushed back, no spills and no other hazards. One patient. Your partner is with you carrying the AED, suction, BVM and oxygen.
firstLookEn: A man standing beside a corner table, red-faced, coughing forcefully and making high-pitched noises, still moving some air in and out. His wife stands beside him in a panic.

primary.locEn: STAGE 1 (partial obstruction) and STAGE 2 (complete obstruction): Alert (AVPU = A). In stage 1 he can only whisper one word, steak; in stage 2 he can make no sound at all. STAGE 3 (collapse, after the engine announces it): unresponsive to voice and to a painful stimulus (AVPU = U). AFTER ROSC (after the engine announces signs of life): drowsy, his eyes open to your voice (AVPU = V); confused, hoarse, and repeats what happened?
primary.airwayEn: STAGE 1 (partial obstruction): noisy, high-pitched air movement - he is still moving some air. STAGE 2 (complete obstruction, after the engine announces that the cough has stopped): no voice, no cough, no air movement. STAGE 3 (collapse): when the candidate opens the airway and looks after 30 compressions, nothing is visible and the breath attempt does not go in (if the head is repositioned and a second attempt is made it still does not go in). LATER AIRWAY CHECK - any look made after the first AED analysis, in the second round of compressions: a piece of steak is now visible at the back of his mouth, pushed up by the compressions; once it is removed under direct vision and the residue is suctioned (adult suction time 10 to 15 seconds), the next breath goes in with air entry. If the candidate sweeps the mouth blindly the examiner gives no finding at all (record blind-finger-sweep). AFTER ROSC: airway open, hoarse voice, no stridor, no food visible. Keep suction at hand.
primary.breathingEn: STAGE 1: forceful cough with noisy air movement. STAGE 2: no air movement. STAGE 3: no chest movement - he is not breathing. DURING THE ARREST: while the steak is in place a BVM breath does not go in; after it is removed and suctioned the next breath goes in with air entry and the chest rises. AFTER ROSC: respirations 22, adequate depth, an occasional cough, equal air entry on both sides.
primary.circulationEn: STAGE 1: radial pulse 120, strong (if rechecked in stage 2, the same). STAGE 3 (collapse): the correct action is chest compressions at once with NO pulse check. If the candidate does check a carotid pulse at the collapse there is no pulse (record the pulse check). AED (give the device prompt only when the candidate turns it on and analyzes): first analysis, after about 2 minutes of CPR - "No shock advised"; second analysis, after a further 2 minutes of CPR - "No shock advised". AFTER the engine announces signs of life (ROSC): carotid and radial pulse 116, strong and regular. Any analysis after ROSC - "No shock advised". A pulse check during the arrest is the circulation assessment, not a vital sign.
primary.rbsEn: Give this once the signs of life are announced: no injury from the lowering, tender over the sternum from the compressions, mild upper abdominal tenderness from the thrusts, no vomit, no medical-alert jewelry. Skin is pale, cool and diaphoretic with pink lips (skin is given automatically during the RBS). If the survey is done during the arrest, the same applies except that tenderness cannot be elicited in an unresponsive patient.
primary.skinEn: STAGE 1: flushed. STAGE 2: lips turning blue. STAGE 3: dusky. AFTER ROSC: pale, cool and diaphoretic, lips pink.

history.ccEn: (Patient, only a whisper while he is still coughing forcefully:) Steak. (Wife:) He choked on a large piece of steak. He swallowed it without chewing and couldn't clear it.

opqrst.oEn: (Wife:) It started about ten past seven. We were having our anniversary dinner, he was talking and laughing, and he swallowed a big piece of steak without chewing it. Then he started coughing.
opqrst.pEn: (Patient, after ROSC, a few words:) It hurts more when I take a deep breath.
opqrst.qEn: (Patient, after ROSC:) It's constant. It never lets up.
opqrst.rEn: (Patient, after ROSC:) My breastbone, and my upper belly. It doesn't go anywhere else. Nothing makes it better. (Wife:) He has never choked before.
opqrst.sEn: (Patient, after ROSC:) My breastbone is about a 6 out of 10 and my upper belly is about a 4.
opqrst.tEn: (Wife:) He started coughing at about ten past seven. (Patient, after ROSC:) The soreness is constant.

history.painScoreEn: Breastbone 6 out of 10, upper abdomen 4 out of 10.

sample.sEn: (Patient, after ROSC:) Sore breastbone, sore upper belly, a scratchy throat, a hoarse voice, a cough, and I feel sick to my stomach.
sample.aEn: (Wife:) Penicillin - it gives him a rash.
sample.mEn: (Wife:) Ramipril and atorvastatin. No blood thinners.
sample.pEn: (Wife:) High blood pressure and high cholesterol. No heart or lung disease, no swallowing problems, and he has never choked before.
sample.lEn: (Wife:) Bread and salad, then the steak, and two glasses of red wine. Nothing since the steak.
sample.eEn: (Wife:) It was our anniversary dinner. He was talking and laughing, swallowed a big piece of steak without chewing, and started coughing and couldn't clear it. The server called, and nobody touched him before you got here. He didn't pass out until he collapsed.

fe.generalEn: I was well all day. I'm tired now.
fe.cnsEn: I'm confused about the last few minutes. No headache, no weakness.
fe.respiratoryEn: My throat's sore and my voice is hoarse. I've got a cough. No wheezing.
fe.cardiovascularEn: My heart's racing now. I had no chest pain before the choking and no palpitations before dinner.
fe.giGuEn: I feel sick to my stomach and my upper belly is sore. I haven't thrown up.
fe.integumentaryEn: Nothing - no problems with my skin.
fe.musculoskeletalEn: My breastbone is sore. No other pain.
fe.eentEn: My throat feels scratchy and swollen. No bleeding in my mouth and no loose teeth.

findings.headNeckEn: Hoarse voice, mild redness at the back of the throat, no swelling, no stridor, trachea midline, no JVD, no scalp injury.
findings.chestLungsEn: Tender over the sternum, no crepitus or deformity, equal air entry on 6-site auscultation, no wheeze.
findings.abdomenEn: Soft, not distended, mild upper tenderness from the thrusts, no guarding.
findings.backEn: No findings; no injury from the lowering.
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: No findings. Pedal pulses present, CSM intact.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: No findings. Radial pulses present, CSM intact.

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: baseline, within 3 minutes of ROSC - the first set; no vital signs exist during the arrest (CPR and the AED come first)
en route, about 6 minutes after set 1 - improving

He suddenly stops coughing. He can't make a sound, and he grabs his throat with both hands.
He goes limp and begins to slump toward the floor.
He goes limp and begins to slump toward the floor.
As the analysis ends he coughs, his eyelids flutter and he takes spontaneous breaths.
He coughs, his eyelids flutter and he takes spontaneous breaths.

expected.actionEn: Acknowledge; plan the AED, suction, BVM and oxygen to the patient's side from the start (the FBAO guideline names suction, AED and BVM) and anticipate that the obstruction may progress to cardiac arrest
triggers: taking the AED, suction and BVM in with us
this may progress to cardiac arrest
I'm planning for a choking call
oxygen, suction and the AED go in with us

expected.actionEn: Brief the partner before arrival: one rescuer takes the airway and chest, the other the AED, suction and BVM
triggers: you take the AED and suction
I'll take the airway and chest
you're on the AED, I'm on compressions
partner has the AED and suction

expected.actionEn: Ask dispatch for first responders as extra hands so compression operators can be changed every 2 minutes (p.10, p.42)
Anticipate saliva, vomit and food debris: plan gloves and eye protection before patient contact
triggers: PPE ready before we reach him

expected.actionEn: Verbalize hazards (none), environment (busy restaurant, crowd, noise), nature of illness (choking on food, suspected FBAO), number of patients (1) and resources (partner with AED, suction, BVM, oxygen)
Don gloves and eye protection
triggers: putting on gloves and eye protection

expected.actionEn: First look: standing, red-faced, coughing with high-pitched noises, still moving some air - a partial obstruction; stay with him
Ask the crowd to give space and use the wife as the information source; identify the route out to the ambulance
triggers: ask the diners to step back

expected.actionEn: Assess LOC / AVPU on contact (Alert, whispering) and again the moment he collapses (Unresponsive to voice and pain)
Verbalize c-spine not indicated (choking, no trauma); with the partner, catch and lower him to the floor in a controlled way so the head and neck are protected
triggers: no trauma so no spinal precautions

expected.actionEn: Separate partial from complete obstruction: while he coughs forcefully, coach him to keep coughing and stay with him; once the cough stops and he cannot speak (universal choking sign) call it a complete obstruction and act at once with abdominal thrusts in sets of five (back slaps or chest thrusts may alternate; chest thrusts if abdominal thrusts are not effective)
Assess breathing: no air movement at stage 2 and no chest movement at stage 3; absent breathing is acted on immediately - thrusts while he is conscious, compressions the moment he collapses
On collapse start chest compressions at once with NO pulse check, and give 30 compressions before the first airway check
Note skin: flushed, then blue lips, then dusky; after ROSC pale, cool, diaphoretic, lips pink
After ROSC complete the rapid body survey (the FBAO pathway ends with 'Complete RBS'): injury from the lowering, tenderness from compressions and thrusts, vomit, medical-alert jewelry
Oxygen through the BVM during the arrest, then 15 L NRB titrated to SpO2 94% or above

Supine on the firm floor for CPR; once he is breathing and drowsy, position to protect the airway (semi-prone / recovery position) with suction ready, and back to supine at once if signs of life are lost
Categorize as RTC and name the criterion: cardiac arrest, unconsciousness / altered LOC and difficulty maintaining the airway (Findings in Unstable Adult Patients, p.7)

Explain why the arrest is worked where he lies: CPR is more effective while stationary, and the reversible cause (airway obstruction) is being cleared on scene, so no loading during active CPR (p.42, p.45)
After ROSC: packaged and ready to load within 15 minutes of arrival (on the cot, straps secured), reassessing ABCs after each move
Delegate under direction: partner on AED, suction and BVM; bystanders and staff to clear the space, bring the cot, hold doors and look after the wife; first responders for extra hands
Establish the chief complaint from the wife: choked on a large piece of steak, progressing to collapse

HxC/C with OPQRRRST / LOTARP: onset about 1910, what he was doing, progression from partial to complete obstruction, who did what before you arrived, loss of consciousness, previous choking episodes, alcohol
triggers: what was he doing when it started

expected.actionEn: Pain score for the sternum and the upper abdomen (6/10 and 4/10) with provoking factor and relief
PMHx (hypertension, high cholesterol; no heart or lung disease, no swallowing problems)
triggers: does he have high blood pressure

expected.actionEn: Medications - ramipril and atorvastatin, no blood thinners (relevant to ibuprofen)
Allergies - penicillin (rash)
LOI - bread, salad and the steak, two glasses of red wine
Use the wife as the history source because the confused patient cannot give a reliable account, and keep her informed
triggers: I'll get the history from his wife

expected.actionEn: GCS with components (13: E3 V4 M6, confused)
BP by auscultation, repeated with each set to trend a post-arrest patient
Pulse rate, strength and rhythm at the radial and carotid
Respirations rate, depth and adequacy - confirm they are adequate and no assisted ventilation is needed
Skin hands-on: temperature, colour, moisture
Pupils
SpO2 on 15 L NRB, target 94% or above
BGL - indicated for a decreased LOC without a known cause
FE - General health
triggers: how have you felt all day

expected.actionEn: FE - CNS (memory gap after a hypoxic episode)
triggers: memory of the last few minutes

expected.actionEn: FE - Respiratory (sore throat, hoarse voice, cough, no wheeze)
FE - Cardiovascular (no chest pain before the choking)
FE - GI/GU (nausea, sore upper abdomen from the thrusts)
FE - Integumentary
FE - Musculoskeletal (sternal soreness from compressions)
FE - Endocrine
FE - EENT (throat, mouth, teeth)
Head/neck exam: voice, throat, neck, trachea, JVD, scalp
Chest exam: palpate the sternum and ribs after compressions, 6-site auscultation with bilateral comparison
Abdomen exam: tenderness from the thrusts, distension
Back exam (during the transfer to the cot)
Lower extremities with CSM
Upper extremities with CSM (PCP: pick the IV site)

Run the FBAO pathway in order: coach the cough while the obstruction is partial; thrusts in sets of five once it is complete; compressions at once on collapse with no pulse check; open the airway and look after 30 compressions; NEVER a blind finger sweep; remove the object only when seen (p.46)
triggers: remove it only if I can see it

expected.actionEn: Asphyxial-arrest AED sequence: the partner applies the AED during one-person CPR, first analysis after 5 cycles (about 2 minutes); no shock advised - resume CPR at once for 2 minutes, analyze and repeat (p.44, p.40)

CPR skill to standard: 30:2, rate 100-120 per minute, depth 5-6 cm, complete recoil, interruptions under 5 seconds, compressions continuing while the AED charges, operators changed every 2 minutes where possible
Airway skill: look in the mouth before each ventilation attempt, reposition the head if the breath does not go in, remove only the object you can see, suction the residue for 10-15 seconds
Breathing skill: BVM with oxygen attached, 2 breaths after each 30 compressions with air entry confirmed and no hyperventilation; after ROSC assist ventilations only if breathing becomes inadequate

Verbalize the analgesia decision: Entonox is contraindicated by altered LOC and inability to comply (p.65); no oral acetaminophen or ibuprofen because he cannot safely swallow; document and reassess pain with each set

Post-ROSC care and re-arrest plan: oxygen titrated to SpO2 94% or above, airway-protecting position with suction ready, and if the signs of life are lost restart compressions at once and let the AED analyze
PCP: vascular access en route as a precaution for re-arrest and any medication, without delaying transport, plus ongoing airway management with suction at hand
Reassess ABCs, the pulse and all interventions after each move and at least every 5 minutes, checking for vomit and keeping suction at hand
Second full set of vitals within 5-6 minutes, interpret the improving trend and reassess the pain
Re-check breathing adequacy at every reassessment and assist ventilations with the BVM if the rate or SpO2 falls (p.11, p.50)
triggers: watch his respiratory rate and SpO2

expected.actionEn: State the re-arrest plan: if the signs of life are lost at any reassessment, restart compressions at once and let the AED analyze
triggers: if he loses signs of life

expected.actionEn: En-route notification for a critical post-arrest patient
Complete hand-off with times: choking onset, collapse, CPR start, AED analyses (no shock advised), object removal, ROSC and both sets of vital signs
State that no shock was advised or delivered and that analgesia was withheld because of the altered LOC
triggers: no shock was advised or delivered
no analgesia because of his altered LOC

expected.actionEn: Accurate PCR within 5 minutes with all event times and the reason analgesia was withheld

specialEvents.descriptionEn: NEUTRAL STAGE DRIVER - record it in the candidate line where EITHER (a) the candidate tells the patient to keep coughing / cough forcefully, or says they ARE coaching the cough and staying with him (an instruction or a statement of what they are doing now - not a plan, and not merely noting that he is coughing), OR (b) the candidate starts thrusts, back slaps or chest thrusts while he is still coughing forcefully (then ALSO record thrusts-while-coughing). The engine then moves the scenario on to the complete obstruction. Never record it when the candidate is only observing or assessing the cough.

BAD ACT: the candidate says they ARE performing (or tells the partner to perform) abdominal thrusts, back slaps or chest thrusts NOW, in a line that comes BEFORE the examiner has delivered the finding that he stops coughing and can make no sound - i.e. while he is still coughing forcefully. Plans and conditionals ("if the cough stops I will...", "while he coughs I coach, once it stops I thrust"), negations, and thrusts made after the examiner's stops-coughing line are NOT this event.

NEUTRAL STAGE DRIVER: the candidate actually delivers (or tells the partner to deliver) a set of abdominal thrusts, back slaps or chest thrusts - present tense, not a plan or a conditional. Record it each time.

BAD ACT: AFTER the examiner has already said that he stopped coughing and can make no sound, the candidate explicitly chooses not to act - for example says they will wait, will only keep encouraging him to cough, or will only watch him - instead of starting thrusts. Not for the candidate line that the examiner's finding was delivered with, and not for a candidate who is simply asking assessment questions.

BAD ACT: the candidate sweeps or hooks the inside of his mouth or throat with a finger when no object has been seen (a blind finger sweep). Removing an object they can SEE under direct vision is NOT this event, and saying they will not do blind sweeps is NOT this event.

BAD ACT: at the collapse, before chest compressions have been started, the candidate checks (or says they are checking) a pulse - carotid or otherwise - or checks breathing and pulse together first. Saying they will NOT check a pulse is not this event; pulse checks after the signs of life are announced are not this event.

BAD ACT: at the collapse the candidate states that they are ventilating, opening the airway and looking, sweeping the mouth, applying the AED or making a call BEFORE any compressions have been given, or says they will start compressions only after that (compressions come first; the first airway check comes after 30 compressions). Do not record for a general reassessment line ("reassessing airway, breathing, circulation") made after compressions were already started or announced, and a pulse check on its own is recorded as pulse-check-on-collapse instead.
candidate applies the AED pads and has it analyze the rhythm during the asphyxial sequence (pads on during CPR, first analysis after about 2 minutes of compressions), personally or by delegating

the SECOND AED analysis of this call, done after the further 2 minutes of CPR that followed the first "no shock advised" analysis. Never record it for the first analysis, and never for pulse checks after signs of life.

in this asphyxial arrest the first analysis is done without about 2 minutes (5 cycles) of CPR first, or compressions are stopped while the pads are put on (the partner should apply the AED during one-person CPR)

BAD ACT: the candidate explicitly decides to leave the AED off, or to wait with it, until the object is out or until the airway has been cleared. Saying the partner will apply it during CPR is NOT this event.

candidate stops compressions for more than about 5 seconds for anything other than the planned airway look and 2 breaths after each 30 compressions and the AED analysis itself - for example hunting for the object, putting on the pads, or a pulse check that lasts longer than 10 seconds
candidate suctions for longer than 15 seconds at a time
candidate verbalizes checking for or seeing chest rise or air entry with the BVM ventilations (or another sign that a ventilation went in)

candidate ventilates clearly faster than the 30:2 ratio allows (e.g. rapid continuous squeezing of the bag, or more than 2 breaths after each 30 compressions), or after ROSC faster than 10-12 per minute

AFTER the examiner has described signs of life (coughing, eyelids flutter, breathing), the candidate says they ARE continuing or restarting chest compressions in a later line without first checking for a pulse, or continues compressions after a pulse has been found. Never record this for the candidate line that the signs-of-life description was answering. Describing CPR standards, a re-arrest plan, or what was done before the signs of life is NOT this event.

AFTER the examiner has reported that his own breathing is adequate (22, adequate depth), the candidate continues or restarts ventilations with the BVM at a set rate. Assisting ventilations only because the breathing later becomes inadequate is NOT this event.
candidate moves the patient onto the stretcher or into the ambulance, or starts transport, while he is still in cardiac arrest (before the signs of life are announced)
an EMR-level candidate inserts a supraglottic airway, starts an IV or gives an IV medication - outside EMR scope. Saying these are outside EMR scope, or that the PCP will do them, is NOT this event.
PCP inserts a supraglottic airway before the obstruction has been cleared, or stops or delays compressions or the AED analysis to insert it before high-quality CPR and the AED are established

drugs.doseEn: WITHHELD in this scenario: Entonox is self-administered by inhalation for relief of pain, but altered level of consciousness and inability to comply are contraindications (p.65) and he is confused (GCS 13). If it is actually given, record drug:entonox.

WITHHELD in this scenario: the usual adult oral dose is 500-1,000 mg PO (p.58), but a confused patient who has just had a complete airway obstruction cannot be trusted to swallow safely. If it is actually given, record drug:acetaminophen.

WITHHELD in this scenario: the usual adult oral dose is 300-400 mg PO (p.68) and he takes no blood thinners, but a confused patient who has just had a complete airway obstruction cannot be trusted to swallow safely. If it is actually given, record drug:ibuprofen.

CPR 30:2 with BVM and oxygen; AED applied by the partner during CPR, two analyses, no shock advised
ROSC at 1925: oxygen 15 L NRB titrated to SpO2 94% or above, airway-protecting position, RTC transport
Entonox and oral analgesics withheld (altered LOC); pain reassessed with each set
PCP: vascular access en route; hospital notified en route
findings: Stage 1 partial obstruction, stage 2 complete obstruction, stage 3 collapse with no chest movement
Baseline after ROSC: GCS 13, BP 158/96, pulse 116, resps 22, SpO2 92% on 15 L, BGL 6.4

examinerPrompts.locNotDepictedEn: At the collapse he does not respond to your voice or to a painful stimulus.
examinerPrompts.breathingNotDepictedEn: At the collapse there is no chest movement.

trackNotes.emrEn: EMR owns the whole call: separating a partial from a complete obstruction, coached coughing, thrusts in sets of five (chest thrusts if abdominal thrusts are not effective), immediate compressions on collapse with no pulse check, airway inspection after 30 compressions with no blind sweeps, suction, 30:2 CPR with a BVM and oxygen, the asphyxial-arrest AED sequence, post-ROSC oxygen titrated to SpO2 94% or above, airway-protecting positioning and RTC transport. Entonox and oral analgesics are withheld (altered LOC); if his GCS had returned to 15 and he could swallow safely, the Appendix A pain rule would apply again - check each drug's contraindications first. No IV, no supraglottic airway, no Functional Enquiry.
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP does everything the EMR does and adds vascular access en route (a precaution for re-arrest and any medication), ongoing airway management with suction at hand (a supraglottic airway only if he re-arrests and high-quality CPR is established), and the 9-system Functional Enquiry en route. (textbook practice - not a BC rubric item) Do not delay compressions, the AED or ventilation to start an IV, and leave the AED pads on and the unit beside the stretcher after ROSC.
